routines.docstring: Validate `changes`, collapse identical replays, and return unique records by ID.

routines.name: read_applied
routines.docstring: Validate the caller-supplied persisted journal and check it names known changes.

routines.name: check_targets
routines.docstring: Reject dependency edges whose target change is absent from the replayed records.

comments: # SPEC: `depends_on`/`applied` default to empty arrays, and any non-array or malformed
# element is `invalid-change`. A bare string is iterable but is not an array, so it is
# rejected here instead of being silently exploded into per-character IDs.
# Replay equality is defined over the *set* of dependencies (SPEC line 11), so ordering
# and repeated edges must not make two otherwise identical records look different.
# `type(...) is not int` rather than isinstance: SPEC excludes booleans, which
# are int subclasses. `units` must be a positive integer.
# Same ID but different component/units/dependency set: the caller is replaying
# an edited record, so neither copy can be trusted as the journal truth.
# Identical replays fall through and collapse to the first copy, so units are
# accounted once; planner sums this mapping, never the raw array.
# An applied entry with no matching change cannot be ordered against the graph,
# so it is a broken journal reference rather than an ignorable extra.
journal.py.moduleNote:
Normalize release records and replay state at the input boundary.

Call direction: planner.py imports this module; journal.py imports nothing local, so it
stays at the bottom of the import chain (policy.py likewise). Membership in the request
body, which records survive replay, and whether edges/journal entries name a known change
are decided here; ordering and budget arithmetic stay in planner.py. Every domain failure
is raised as JournalError whose message is the wire error code, so planner.py can assemble
the single error shape without re-mapping codes.

routines.name: topological_order
routines.docstring:
Return change IDs in deterministic dependency order.

The eligible set is kept in a heap so the smallest ID is always taken first; this is
what makes replay deterministic across runs and across Python builds (a plain set
iteration would vary). Callers must have run `check_targets` first, so every edge here
points at a known ID.

comments: # Some node never became ready, which for a finite digraph means a cycle. It is
# checked after the full sweep so a cycle anywhere fails the request even when a
# cycle-free prefix could already have been ordered.
# Only applied changes roll back, and the full order is reversed *before* filtering
# so dependents are undone before the things they depend on. Budget is not a cap
# here (SPEC line 14): capping would silently truncate a release history.
# plan: applied entries satisfy dependencies but ship already, so they consume no new
# budget; the cap is applied to the emitted set only, after replay/dedup.
# Checked after the emitted set is known, so budget comparisons use post-replay units.
planner.py.moduleNote:
Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

Import direction is planner -> {journal, policy} and must stay that way: journal and policy
never import planner, so they cannot assemble a result or reach back into ordering. This
module alone owns graph order, budget arithmetic and the single ok/error result shape.

Failure discipline: every domain problem is raised by a callee and converted here into
the exact error shape with empty `actions` and `units` 0, so a rejected request can never
leak a partial action list (SPEC line 7).

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring:
Return the validated budget.

For `rollback` the budget is still validated (SPEC line 14) but is never used as a cap
by planner, because a rollback must be able to describe the whole applied history.

comments: # G1: both environments support both actions, so the sets are the whole authorization
# rule; widening one of them later is the only place that needs to change.
# Test membership as `isinstance(value, str) and value in ENVIRONMENTS`, never as a bare
# `value not in ENVIRONMENTS`: list/dict values are unhashable, so the set lookup would
# raise TypeError and escape as a crash instead of the SPEC `invalid-environment` result.
# `type(...) is not int`: SPEC excludes booleans, which are int subclasses.
policy.py.moduleNote:
Validate release policy before computing actions.

Called only by planner.py (import direction: planner -> {journal, policy}). policy owns
the request-level gates (environment, action, budget) and knows nothing about records or
ordering; rollback eligibility is a policy question, while *which* applied changes get
emitted is decided by planner from the graph.

routines.name: read_retain
routines.docstring:
Validate the G2 rollback `retain` list and return it as a frozenset of IDs.

CHANGE-G2 line 3: `retain` names already-applied changes that must stay. It is only a
rollback concept -- policy.py has already rejected everything but staging plan/rollback
before this runs, and planner.py calls this only on the rollback path, so a `plan` request
carrying `retain` keeps G1 behaviour and never fails because of that extra field.

Every malformed `retain` is `invalid-retain`, deliberately *not* `unknown-dependency`: an
unknown or non-applied ID here means the caller named something it cannot retain, so the
list itself is rejected rather than being treated as a broken journal reference.

comments: # SPEC: `depends_on`/`applied` default to empty arrays, and any non-array or malformed
# element is `invalid-change`. A bare string is iterable but is not an array, so it is
# rejected here instead of being silently exploded into per-character IDs.
# Replay equality is defined over the *set* of dependencies (SPEC line 11), so ordering
# and repeated edges must not make two otherwise identical records look different.
# `type(...) is not int` rather than isinstance: SPEC excludes booleans, which
# are int subclasses. `units` must be a positive integer.
# Same ID but different component/units/dependency set: the caller is replaying
# an edited record, so neither copy can be trusted as the journal truth.
# Identical replays fall through and collapse to the first copy, so units are
# accounted once; planner sums this mapping, never the raw array.
# An applied entry with no matching change cannot be ordered against the graph,
# so it is a broken journal reference rather than an ignorable extra.
# Do not reuse `_id_list`: it raises `invalid-change`, and the retain list has its own code.
# A bare string is iterable but is not an array, so it is rejected instead of being
# exploded into per-character IDs.
# Catches both unknown IDs and known-but-not-applied ones: retaining a change that
# is not in the journal is meaningless and would silently protect nothing.

routines.name: retained_closure
routines.docstring:
Return the applied IDs a rollback must keep: `retain` plus their applied dependencies.

CHANGE-G2 line 3. The walk follows `depends_on` transitively, but only into already
applied changes: a dependency that is not applied is not part of the release history, so
it is neither emitted nor retained. `check_targets` has already run, so every edge names
a known change and the recursion terminates. Callers must have validated `retain` against
`applied` first (journal.read_retain), so the seeds are all applied.

comments: # Some node never became ready, which for a finite digraph means a cycle. It is
# checked after the full sweep so a cycle anywhere fails the request even when a
# cycle-free prefix could already have been ordered.
# Only applied changes roll back, and the full order is reversed *before* filtering
# so dependents are undone before the things they depend on. Budget is not a cap
# here (SPEC line 14): capping would silently truncate a release history.
# Compute the retained closure on the full graph (edges may point at non-applied
# changes; retained_closure filters those) and drop it from the emitted set. The
# surrounding order is untouched, so the remaining applied IDs keep the original
# deterministic reverse order required by CHANGE-G2 line 3.
# plan: applied entries satisfy dependencies but ship already, so they consume no new
# budget; the cap is applied to the emitted set only, after replay/dedup. G2 line 2: the
# cap is already the effective one (min(request budget, staging quota)) from policy, so
# comparing against it here covers a caller that grants more than the quota allows.
# Checked after the emitted set is known, so budget comparisons use post-replay units.
planner.py.moduleNote:
Compose policy and journal data into a plan.

Import direction is planner -> {journal, policy} and must stay that way: journal and policy
never import planner, so they cannot assemble a result or reach back into ordering. This

Failure discipline: every domain problem is raised by a callee and converted here into

routines.name: limit_for
routines.docstring:
Validate environment/action/budget and return the effective per-request budget.

For `rollback` the budget is still validated (SPEC line 14) but is never used as a cap
by planner, because a rollback must be able to describe the whole applied history; the
value returned here is therefore ignored for rollback.

For `plan` the returned value is the effective cap: the smaller of the request budget and
STAGING_PLAN_QUOTA (CHANGE-G2 line 2). The request budget itself is still validated by the
G1 rule, so a caller asking for 5 is not itself an error -- exceeding 3 units is.

comments: # G2: this release is staging-only. `production` stays a *known* environment so it can be
# reported as frozen (`production-frozen`) instead of an unknown-value error; the default-deny
# sets below stay the whole authorization rule and are the only place to change later.
# `ACTIONS` is still used to validate the request action even under the production gate, so a
# frozen request with a bogus action is still reported as frozen, never as a partial action.
# G2 line 2: a staging plan may ship at most 3 units no matter what the request budget allows.
# Kept here (policy owns budget) and consumed by planner as a plain cap.
# Test membership as `isinstance(value, str) and value in ENVIRONMENTS`, never as a bare
# `value not in ENVIRONMENTS`: list/dict values are unhashable, so the set lookup would
# raise TypeError and escape as a crash instead of the SPEC `invalid-environment` result.
# G2 line 1: the production freeze is decided here, before action/budget validation and
# before journal.py touches any record or planner.py builds the graph. That ordering is
# what makes a malformed or cyclic graph on production still report `production-frozen`,
# and it guarantees no partial actions can be produced for a frozen environment.
# Unknown environments are rejected above, so an unknown value never reaches this gate.
# `type(...) is not int`: SPEC excludes booleans, which are int subclasses.
